title: Leverage and margin

inOneLine.simple: Leverage lets a small deposit, called margin, hold a big trade. It makes losses bigger as well as gains.
inOneLine.balanced: Required [[margin]] = trade value ÷ [[leverage]], converted to your account currency. Leverage changes the deposit needed, not the profit or loss per pip.

explain.simple: With leverage, your broker lets you open a trade much bigger than the money you put down. The money set aside is called margin. At 1:30 leverage, 1 dollar of margin holds 30 dollars of trade. Your profit or loss is based on the full trade size, not on the margin. So a small move in price can make a large dent in your account. Margin is a deposit. It is not the most you can lose.
explain.balanced: Required margin = units × price (in the quote currency) ÷ leverage, then converted into the account currency. Leverage limits are set by brokers and, in many places, by regulators, and they can differ between instruments. Higher leverage means less margin per trade, which makes it easy to open trades that are too big. Risk is set by size and stop distance, not by leverage, but leverage is what lets oversized trades happen. Losses can exceed the margin, and in some cases the account balance.

assumptions: Illustrative prices and leverage, not any broker's actual terms
steps: A 100-pip move against you = 100 × 1 = 100 USD lost, more than a quarter of the margin.
A 100-pip move for you = 100 USD gained. Leverage magnifies both directions.
The base currency is USD, so the trade value is already 10,000 USD.
If the same trade used 1:20 leverage instead, margin = 10,000 ÷ 20 = 500 USD.
The profit or loss per pip is the same in both cases: 10,000 × 0.01 = 100 JPY, about 0.67 USD at 150.00.

explainSimpler: Leverage is like putting down a small deposit on something big. If its price falls, you lose on the whole thing, not just the deposit.
commonMistake: Thinking that margin is the most you can lose, or that high leverage is a free bonus. Margin is only the deposit. Losses come from the full trade size, and with high leverage it is easy to open a trade far too big for the account.

quickCheck.prompt: GBP/USD at 1.2500, 0.10 lot (10,000 GBP), leverage 1:50, account in USD. What margin is required?

options.explanation: No: that uses 10,000 without converting GBP to USD first.
No: that is the full trade value, before leverage.

quickCheck.prompt: Which statement about leverage is true?

options.text: It magnifies losses as well as gains
options.explanation: Right: profit and loss come from the full trade size, in both directions.

options.text: It limits your loss to the margin
options.explanation: No: losses can be larger than the margin.
No: a move against you is magnified in exactly the same way.

doItNow.instructions: Open the margin calculator. For each trade on your list of 10, enter the pair, size, price, leverage and account currency, and write down the required margin. Do at least two by hand first.

homework: Finish your list of 10 trades with pip value and required margin for each. Include at least two pairs where the account currency is not the quote currency.
